newsitem.title: FRANCE: Divisions out in the open in French snap campaign.
newsitem.headline: Divisions out in the open in French snap campaign.

text.p: Just a week into France's snap election campaign, painfully-concealed divisions within both the ruling centre-right coalition and its left-wing foe have suddenly burst to the surface.

On the right, maverick Euro-critic Philippe Seguin denounced what he called the ultra-liberal (free-marketeer) logic of the rush to European monetary union on the day the ruling coalition published a purposefully vague manifesto.

On the left, Socialist and Communist leaders Lionel Jospin and Robert Hue agreed on an election agreement which they were at pains to insist was not a pact for government. Differences over plans for a single European currency were glossed over.

Distancing himself from fellow Gaullist Prime Minister Alain Juppe's programme, National Assembly speaker Seguin said the fight against unemployment should be at the heart of the campaign and at the centre of government policy.

He lamented that in response to rising unemployment, "people everywhere are mouthing words that seem meaningless: convergence criteria, flexibility, globalisation, federalism". Such slogans were "alibis for inaction disguised as promises of a radiant future", he said.

Jospin seized on Seguin's broadside. "Far better to have different groups assume their differences, and debate them before the French, rather than a facade of unity as I believe the right has today," he said.

Similarly, Juppe derided the pact reached by the Socialists and Communists as "demagogic" on public spending, "very backward-looking" on the public sector, "very interventionist" on working hours, "verbose" on Europe and lax on illegal immigration.

In a platform entitled "A new impulse for France", the centre-right had pledged to stabilise public spending, pursue tax cuts and promote talks on shorter working hours if, as polls predict, it wins the May 25-June 1 parliamentary election.
Juppe said a re-elected government would present to parliament in its first 40 days a five-year plan for holding the increase in public spending to less than the rate of inflation.
Defending the lack of specifics, Juppe told a news conference: "We are not running a campaign for accountants."
The pact unveiled by Jospin and Hue pledged a shift to a 35-hour working week without loss of pay, the creation of 700,000 youth jobs and a halt to privatisation.

The latest opinion poll released on Tuesday suggested the government held only a slim lead over the left in voting intentions and would win a reduced majority of National Assembly seats, confirming a series of surveys over the last week.
A CSA institute poll suggested the coalition's lead over the left had narrowed in the last week to about 40 seats in the 577-seat Assembly.

It forecast the centre-right would win 296, the Socialists and ecologists 237, the Communists 21 and the extreme-right National Front one of the 555 seats in metropolitan France. Coalition supporters hold most of the 22 seats in overseas departments and territories.
Another poll on Tuesday found widespread indifference among voters, more than one-third of whom said that neither the centre-right nor the left would address their concerns. REUTER
